newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian court to rule whether "British spy" sane.
newsitem.headline: Russian court to rule whether "British spy" sane.

text.p: Russian judges met behind closed doors on Monday to decide whether a junior foreign ministry official alleged to have spied for Britain is mentally fit to stand trial, Russian media said.

Interfax news agency quoted sources at the Moscow City Court as saying criminal proceedings against Platon Obukhov, 28, could be dropped if the court decides he is mentally unfit -- as his father, a former top diplomat, asserts.

Court officials could not be reached for comment on the case, which Russian security officials have trumpeted as a great success in a new East-West spy game being played with scarcely less intensity than during the Cold War.

Obukhov was a second secretary in the ministry's prestigious North America Department who wrote pulp spy thrillers on the side. He has been in prison since his arrest last April on charges that he was paid for information by British MI6 agents.
Obukhov's lawyer and his parents insist he has been mentally unstable since childhood and is unfit to stand trial. They want him discharged to a psychiatric hospital.
However, the Federal Security Service (FSB) insists that Obukhov was quite sane while he was spying and that his illness cannot and should not free him from facing the court.
If the court rules Obukhov was sane at the time of the alleged crime and is capable in principle of facing charges, he will be admitted to hospital and tried when he recovers.
Psychiatric tests in 1996 and 1997 confirmed Obukhov was ill but did not rule out that he had been sane while spying. Itar-Tass news agency said Obukhov had "reactive psychosis".
Tass quoted Alexander Zdanovich, the FSB's chief spokesman, as saying he expected a trial to take place soon.
Obukhov, son of a former Soviet deputy foreign minister and top disarmament negotiator, admitted last year that he had spied for Britain's MI6 intelligence service.
He was shown, wearing unmatched socks, admitting the charges in a television interview. "Before and after each contact I vomited. I could not eat. I was in panicky fear," he said.
It was not clear how much classified information he had access to. His parents insist he had no access to it at all.
Yet several Russian media, playing up the FSB's catch, compared Obukhov to the "giants of espionage", saying he had been in personal contact with senior British agents in Moscow.
Soon after Obukhov's arrest, several diplomats at the British embassy in Moscow were expelled, accused of links to a Russian citizen who had access to classified information.
In a Cold War-style tit-for-tat response, Britain expelled some Russian embassy officials.
The FSB says it caught 27 professional foreign spies last year and 60 Russians in the pay of foreign powers.
It also claimed great success for an FSB telephone hotline, set up last month to invite Russians spying for foreign countries to turn themselves in and become double agents.
The head of the FSB said recently foreign spy services were very active in Russia and that he was shocked by how cheaply many Russians were prepared to sell out their country.

Treason, until last year a capital offence, now carries a maximum sentence of 20 years plus confiscation of assets. Two Russians were sentenced in the past month to terms of seven and 10 years hard labour, one for spying for the United States, the other for Britain. Both their sentences took account of the fact that they cooperated with their interrogators, officials said.
